body:
Why Stronger Rulers Needed More Resources

The growth of territorial kingship increased the demand for material resources. Rulers needed to support attendants, priests, military followers and other people associated with their authority.

Pastoral communities could provide livestock and occasional gifts, but settled agriculture created opportunities to obtain a share of production more regularly.

As cultivators produced grain over successive agricultural seasons, rulers could claim a portion of that output. This created the basis for increasingly organised systems of revenue collection.

Bali: From Offering Towards Levy

The term bali is important because its meaning and political significance changed over time.

In the early Vedic period, bali largely represented a voluntary or occasional contribution to the tribal chief. It was not associated with a developed tax-collection bureaucracy.

During the later Vedic period, contributions to rulers increasingly acquired an obligatory character in some political contexts. Bali could function as a levy rather than merely an expression of voluntary support.

However, this does not establish that every later Vedic kingdom possessed a uniform or fully developed taxation system. The transition towards compulsory revenue demands was gradual.

Important Revenue Terms

TermPrincipal MeaningImportant Qualification
BaliOffering, tribute or developing levyInitially largely voluntary; increasingly obligatory in later contexts
BhagaA share of agricultural produce or revenueAssociated with the ruler's claim over production
Shulka or SulkaLevy or duty, often associated with goods and exchangeMust not be confused with agricultural produce itself

The relationship between these terms and actual revenue practices differed across periods and political communities.

Do Not Transfer a Later Tax Rate Backwards

In descriptions of the mahajanapadas, the ruler's agricultural share or bhaga is commonly stated as 1/6 of the produce.

That figure should not be treated as a proven, universal taxation rate for every later Vedic kingdom. More systematic revenue collection belongs particularly to the subsequent development of territorial states.

The Appearance of More Specialised Functionaries

As political organisation became more complex, rulers required assistance from people performing different functions.

Later Vedic literature mentions a group of important persons called ratnins, literally the valued or jewelled ones. They were associated with the ruler and royal ceremonies.

Some titles connected with this developing political organisation include:

  • Purohita: The priest associated with royal rituals and advice.
  • Senani or Senapati: A leader of the fighting force.
  • Gramani: A leader associated with a grama or village community.
  • Suta: A charioteer associated with the ruler and the narration of his achievements.
  • Bhagadugha: A person associated with the collection or apportionment of shares.
  • Sangrahitri: A functionary associated with the gathering or management of resources, often described as a treasurer.
  • Akshavapa: A functionary associated with dice or gaming in the royal setting.

These terms illustrate increasing specialisation around the ruler. Nevertheless, ritual participants and royal attendants were not necessarily permanent civil servants. The existence of such titles does not prove that later Vedic kingdoms already possessed a complete salaried bureaucracy.

Military Development

The early Vedic fighting force depended largely on the mobilisation of tribal members.

During the later Vedic period, military organisation became more important as rulers sought to defend settlements and assert territorial authority. Yet a permanent, centrally maintained army was not necessarily present in every developing kingdom.

Regularly supported armies and more organised bureaucracies became clearer features of some mahajanapadas from approximately the 6th century BCE.

Prelims focus

  • Bali: An early offering that gradually developed towards tribute or taxation.
  • Bhaga: Share of produce or revenue.
  • Shulka: A levy or duty associated with exchange.
  • Ratnins: Important persons associated with the ruler and royal rituals.
  • Bhagadugha: Associated with collecting or apportioning shares.
  • Sangrahitri: Associated with gathering or managing resources.
  • Trap: The appearance of royal functionaries does not automatically mean the existence of a complete permanent bureaucracy.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, 2018–19, Chapter 5, pp. 46–47, and Chapter 6, pp. 58–59; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, Kings, Farmers and Towns, pp. 29–31; National Institute of Open Schooling, History (315), Lesson 4, sections 4.10–4.11, pp. 57–59; IGNOU, Administrative and Institutional Systems in North India, Unit 16, section 16.2, pp. 21–22; IGNOU, Political Structures in India, MHI-104, Unit 2, Territorial States to Empire, section 2.3, consulted through eGyankosh on 17 November 2026.]

title: Tribute, Taxation and the Beginnings of Administration

body:
The Growth of Social Differentiation

The growing importance of settled agriculture, territorial kingship and elaborate rituals was accompanied by changes in social organisation.

Social distinctions became more clearly expressed through the varna system, which classified society into 4 broad categories. These categories were associated with particular duties, occupations and ritual privileges.

The later Vedic period was important in the development of this framework, although the more elaborate rules found in later Brahmanical legal texts should not automatically be assumed to describe every actual social practice of the Vedic age.

The Four Varnas

Brahmanas

Brahmanas were associated with religious learning, teaching the Vedas and performing sacrifices.

As royal rituals became more elaborate, the services of trained priests gained importance. Brahmanas received gifts and claimed high ritual status.

Kshatriyas

Kshatriyas were associated with rulership, warfare and the protection of political communities.

As kingship grew stronger, ruling families increasingly claimed Kshatriya status. Their authority rested on political and military power, while Brahmanas provided religious support through rituals and social teachings.

Vaishyas

Vaishyas were associated with agriculture, animal husbandry, trade and other productive activities.

The growth of agriculture made producing communities increasingly important to the economic foundation of kingship. Rulers and priests could receive gifts, tribute and other resources from such groups.

Shudras

Shudras occupied the lowest position within the prescribed four-varna hierarchy and were assigned service to the other 3 varnas in priestly formulations.

These prescriptions imposed restrictions on their participation in certain Vedic rituals and forms of Vedic learning.

Varna and Birth

Later Vedic social thought increasingly connected varna status with birth. Brahmanical texts presented different duties and privileges for members of the four groups.

However, a distinction must be maintained between what a text prescribed and what people actually practised. The subcontinent contained diverse communities and occupations, and not every community necessarily accepted or followed the same social rules.

The four-varna classification also should not be confused with the numerous specific hereditary jatis or caste communities familiar from later periods.

Ritual Privileges and Social Rank

An important distinction concerned access to Vedic education and ritual participation.

In Brahmanical prescriptions, the first 3 varnas were entitled to upanayana, an initiation associated with Vedic study. They consequently came to be described as dvija, or twice-born.

Shudras were excluded from this privilege under these rules. Restrictions also affected women's access to Vedic study and certain rituals.

These distinctions reveal how ritual privileges contributed to social hierarchy.

Family and Gotra

The family remained the basic social institution. Larger households including several generations became important in the increasingly settled society.

Patrilineal principles, which traced descent through the father's line, were significant in family and inheritance practices.

The institution of gotra also developed. A gotra was associated with descent from a common ancestor, often identified with a Vedic seer.

Brahmanical marriage rules increasingly favoured marriage outside one's own gotra. This practice is called gotra exogamy.

Such rules expressed an ideal of kinship organisation. Their application varied across communities and periods.

Changes in the Position of Women

Later Vedic texts increasingly emphasised patriarchal family authority and placed restrictions on women's participation in some public and ritual activities.

Women were generally expected to become members of their husband's household after marriage. Male descent and the importance attached to sons gained emphasis in many ritual and family contexts.

Nevertheless, these changes should not be presented as the complete disappearance of women's intellectual, social or religious roles. The surviving texts represent particular traditions and do not describe every community equally.

Varna Rules and Actual Society

The four-varna system described an increasingly influential social ideal. It did not automatically determine the occupation, status or behaviour of every person in every region. Social rank, wealth, political power and lived practices could differ from prescribed categories.

Prelims focus

  • Brahmanas: Priestly learning and ritual functions.
  • Kshatriyas: Rulership and warfare.
  • Vaishyas: Agriculture, animal husbandry and trade.
  • Shudras: Service functions in the prescribed four-varna hierarchy.
  • Upanayana: Initiation associated with Vedic study.
  • Dvija: Twice-born, applied to the first 3 varnas in Brahmanical rules.
  • Gotra exogamy: Marriage outside one's own gotra.
  • Trap: Normative descriptions of varna should not be mistaken for a complete account of actual society.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, 2018–19, Chapter 6, pp. 55–56; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 3, Kinship, Caste and Class, pp. 55–62; National Institute of Open Schooling, History (315), Lesson 4, sections 4.6–4.7, pp. 53–55, consulted 17 November 2026.]

title: Later Vedic Society: Varna, Kinship and Increasing Social Stratification

body:
What Makes a Territorial State Different from a Tribe?

A tribal community is primarily united through recognised kinship and common identity. A territorial state, by contrast, exercises political authority over a defined region and the population living within it.

The distinction is not simply whether a community has a leader. Both tribal communities and territorial states may have rulers. The important difference concerns the organisation of authority and resources.

A more developed territorial state generally possesses a recognisable territory, a ruling institution, mechanisms for obtaining resources, officials performing administrative functions and the ability to organise military power.

The Janapada Stage

During the later Vedic period, communities increasingly became associated with settled territories known as janapadas.

Kuru and Panchala were among the important political regions in the Ganga-Yamuna area. Kosala and Videha were also significant in the eastward development of political and cultural institutions.

This stage was characterised by stronger kingship, the increasing importance of agriculture and the development of more elaborate social and ritual structures.

Nevertheless, not every janapada possessed all the institutions of a mature state.

The Rise of Mahajanapadas

From approximately the 6th century BCE, larger territorial states became prominent in northern India. These are commonly known as mahajanapadas, meaning great janapadas.

Buddhist and Jaina texts refer to 16 mahajanapadas, although the lists do not agree completely.

Prominent names include Magadha, Kosala, Vajji, Kuru, Panchala, Gandhara and Avanti.

Fortified Capitals

Many mahajanapadas possessed capital cities, and a number of these capitals were fortified. Fortifications could provide protection, demonstrate royal power and make important settlements easier to control.

Regular Revenue and Military Organisation

Building fortifications, maintaining officials and supporting armies required substantial resources.

Some rulers therefore developed more systematic methods of taxation. Agricultural produce became a major source of revenue, while other contributions could come from crafts, animal husbandry, trade and forest products.

In textbook descriptions of the mahajanapada period, the ruler's agricultural share, or bhaga, is commonly given as 1/6 of production.

Some states developed standing armies and more regular administrative structures. These features distinguish the mahajanapada age from the earlier Vedic system of tribal mobilisation and occasional contributions.

Monarchies and Gana-Sanghas

Most mahajanapadas were monarchies, where a king exercised political authority. However, some had different arrangements.

A gana-sangha was a political organisation in which authority was shared among several leading members, often collectively called rajas.

Vajji, associated with Vaishali in present-day Bihar, is a well-known example.

In such systems, leading members met in assemblies and discussed political and military matters. However, participation was restricted. Women, enslaved people and many labouring groups were excluded from political decision-making.

Therefore, these systems should not be equated with modern democracies based on universal adult suffrage.

Two Different Uses of Collective Institutions

Early Vedic sabha and samiti: Assemblies associated with tribal political consultation.

Later gana-sangha: A non-monarchical political organisation in which several leading members shared authority.

Both involved collective participation, but they belonged to different political contexts and should not be treated as identical institutions.

Magadha as an Example of a Powerful Mahajanapada

Magadha became an important example of the growing strength of territorial states during the 6th–4th centuries BCE.

Its advantages included fertile agricultural land, access to the Ganga and its tributaries, forest resources including elephants, and access to iron-producing regions.

Rulers such as Bimbisara and Ajatasattu strengthened Magadhan power through political and military expansion.

The earlier capital was Rajagriha, also called Rajagaha and identified with present-day Rajgir in Bihar. The capital was later shifted to Pataliputra, near the Ganga, in the 4th century BCE.

These developments belong to the subsequent age of larger territorial states rather than to the Early Vedic period.

The Overall Political Transformation

The transformation from tribal society to territorial states involved several interconnected developments. Increasingly settled agriculture strengthened the economic foundation of political authority. Royal succession and ceremonies helped rulers establish their position. Tribute and taxation developed as means of obtaining resources. Administrative specialists and military institutions gradually became more important.

By the mahajanapada period, some political communities possessed recognisable capital cities, more developed revenue systems and stronger military organisations.

Prelims focus

  • Jana: A tribe or people.
  • Janapada: Territorial settlement associated with a jana.
  • Mahajanapada: A large territorial state.
  • 16 mahajanapadas: Mentioned in early Buddhist and Jaina textual traditions.
  • Vajji: An important example of a gana-sangha, associated with Vaishali.
  • Magadha: A powerful mahajanapada associated initially with Rajagriha and later with Pataliputra.
  • Trap: A gana-sangha was not necessarily a democracy in the modern sense.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, 2018–19, Chapter 6, pp. 56–61; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, Kings, Farmers and Towns, pp. 29–31; National Institute of Open Schooling, History (315), Lesson 4, section 4.11, pp. 58–59; IGNOU, Administrative and Institutional Systems in North India, Unit 16, sections 16.2–16.3, pp. 21–22, consulted 17 November 2026.]
